node.label: Medical & health history
node.date_label: Earlier medical scholarship · social-medicine interventions 1930s · later social histories · coverage through 2000
node.description: Studies medicine, illness, healing and health in their historical settings. Practitioner scholarship, institutional histories, patient perspectives, public health and colonial or gendered experience coexist and contest what should count as medical knowledge and whose records matter.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Henry E. Sigerist: Socialized Medicine in the Soviet Union (1937); Roy Porter: “Lay Medical Knowledge” (1985); Dorothy Porter: Health, Civilization and the State (1999); Barbara Duden: The Woman Beneath the Skin (English edition 1991); Megan Vaughan: Curing Their Ills (1991); Steven Feierman: The Social Basis of Health and Healing in Africa (1992); John M. Janzen: The Social Basis of Health and Healing in Africa (1992).

node.scope_note: An enduring field with several programmes, not a school founded by the Society for the Social History of Medicine or its 1988 journal. Sigerist prevents a simple doctors-to-social-historians replacement story. Africa is represented by distinct projects, not a regional proxy. Asian, Latin American and Indigenous medical historiographies, clinical scholarship and histories of psychiatry require fuller treatment.

strands.title: Hygienic Modernity: Meanings of Health and Disease in Treaty-Port China

strands.title: The persistence of history: Racism, anti-Blackness, and the causes of mental ill health, c.1800–2020
strands.focus: Wynter, Campbell, Chaney and Marks historicize changing explanations of mental illness while tracing the persistence of racialized assumptions. Wynter and coauthors widen the history of antiracist psychiatry by examining Frederick Hickling, Aggrey Burke and Suman Fernando alongside better-known figures. Version-of-record opening pp. 2–3 checked; attribution to this historical analysis, not clinical guidance or endorsement of historical racial categories. Selected programme passage pp. 2–3; clinicians are subjects of the 2025 study, not its coauthors. Their careers are not dated 2025.
strands.works: The persistence of history: Racism, anti-Blackness, and the causes of mental ill health, c.1800–2020

node.label: Spatial history / Historical geography
node.date_label: Sauer 1925 · Hoskins 1955 · critical spatial studies and historical GIS by the 1990s · coverage through 2000
node.description: Investigates how places, landscapes, territories and spatial relationships are made and transformed through time. Reconstructing past geographies, interpreting maps and colonial naming, tracing contested place identities, and linking historical records through GIS are different practices within this broad field.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Carl O. Sauer: “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925); H. C. Darby: Domesday England (1977); W. G. Hoskins: The Making of the English Landscape (1955); J. B. Harley: “Deconstructing the Map” (1989); Doreen Massey: “Places and Their Pasts” (1995); Felix Driver: “Rethinking the Idea of Place” (1995), with Samuel; Raphael Samuel: “Rethinking the Idea of Place” (1995), with Driver; Dolores Hayden: The Power of Place (1995); Paul Carter: The Road to Botany Bay (1987); Ian N. Gregory: “Putting the past in its place” (1998), with Southall; Humphrey Southall: “Putting the past in its place” (1998), with Gregory.

node.scope_note: Historical geography has roots well before digital mapping. Spatial history is an overlapping set of approaches, not a synonym for GIS or one unified school. The existing Geography & environmental inquiry entry retains its wider intellectual resources. This selection foregrounds British reconstruction, Australian colonial space and a British HGIS project; wider regional traditions and Indigenous spatial knowledge require fuller treatment. Later digital projects are not backdated into coverage through 2000.
